The binomial distribution

Hit or miss, again and again, independently of each other: a multiple-choice test where you guess. An airline that sells more tickets than it has seats. A delivery in which a few parts are faulty. Behind all of this is the same distribution. With a single formula and a histogram you answer questions like “How likely are at most two errors?”.

20 LESSONS3 UNITS1 LAB
WHAT YOU WILL LEARN IN THIS CHAPTER
  • recognise Bernoulli trials and Bernoulli chains
  • count paths with the factorial and the binomial coefficient
  • calculate single and cumulative probabilities with Bernoulli's formula, also with a table and a calculator
  • use the expected value $n \cdot p$ and the standard deviation and interpret histograms

UNIT 16 LESSONS

1Bernoulli chains and Bernoulli's formula

A dice is rolled five times. How likely is a six exactly twice?

A path with exactly two sixes, for example 66NNN, has the probability $\left(\tfrac16\right)^2 \cdot \left(\tfrac56\right)^3$. How many such paths are there? You have to choose 2 of the 5 rolls for the sixes: 66NNN, 6N6NN, …, NNN66. That is 10 possibilities. So $P(X = 2) = 10 \cdot \tfrac{1}{36} \cdot \tfrac{125}{216} \approx 0.161$.

KEY POINT · BERNOULLI CHAIN AND BINOMIAL DISTRIBUTION

A Bernoulli trial has exactly two outcomes: hit (probability $p$) and miss ($1 - p$). A Bernoulli chain of length $n$ consists of $n$ independent repetitions with the same $p$.

The binomial coefficient $\binom{n}{k} = \dfrac{n!}{k! \cdot (n - k)!}$ counts the paths with exactly $k$ hits, with $n! = 1 \cdot 2 \cdot \ldots \cdot n$ and $0! = 1$.

Bernoulli's formula: for the number $X$ of hits $$P(X = k) = \binom{n}{k} \cdot p^k \cdot (1 - p)^{n - k}.$$ $X$ is then called binomially distributed with the parameters $n$ and $p$.

Calculator: there $\binom{n}{k}$ is usually called nCr, the binomial distribution binompdf (single) and binomcdf (cumulative).

Drawing without replacement is not a Bernoulli chain, because $p$ changes from draw to draw. With large numbers, though, it almost is one.

INTERACTIVE · ALL PATHS WITH EXACTLY k HITS

Choose the length of the chain, the number of hits $k$ and $p$. The glowing paths are counted: that is $\binom{n}{k}$.

EXAMPLE 1 · THE GUESSING TEST

10 questions, 4 answers each, one correct, everything guessed. How likely are exactly 3 correct answers? How likely is none?

$n = 10$, $p = 0.25$: $P(X = 3) = \binom{10}{3} \cdot 0.25^3 \cdot 0.75^7 = 120 \cdot 0.015625 \cdot 0.1335 \approx 0.250$

$P(X = 0) = 0.75^{10} \approx 0.056$

EXAMPLE 2 · BINOMIAL COEFFICIENTS

Calculate $\binom{5}{2}$, $\binom{7}{3}$ and $\binom{49}{6}$. What does the last one count?

$\binom52 = \tfrac{5 \cdot 4}{2 \cdot 1} = 10$, $\binom73 = \tfrac{7 \cdot 6 \cdot 5}{3 \cdot 2 \cdot 1} = 35$, $\binom{49}{6} = 13{,}983{,}816$: the number of possible tickets in the German lottery “6 out of 49”.

EXERCISES

Is this a Bernoulli chain? If so, give $n$ and $p$. a) roll a dice 20 times, hit: six   b) draw 3 of 5 raffle tickets without replacement   c) check 50 parts, 2% rejects

a) yes, $n = 20$, $p = \tfrac16$   b) no, $p$ changes   c) yes (approximately, for a large production), $n = 50$, $p = 0.02$

Calculate $\binom{6}{2}$, $\binom{8}{4}$ and $\binom{10}{0}$.

15, 70, 1

A coin is tossed 10 times. How likely are exactly five heads? Why is that not so likely after all?

$\binom{10}{5} \cdot 0.5^{10} = \tfrac{252}{1024} \approx 0.246$. “Exactly 5” is only one of 11 possible values, the neighbours 4 and 6 are almost as likely.

Roll a dice 12 times. How likely are exactly two sixes?

$\binom{12}{2} \cdot \left(\tfrac16\right)^2 \cdot \left(\tfrac56\right)^{10} = 66 \cdot \tfrac{1}{36} \cdot 0.1615 \approx 0.296$

Use paths to explain why $\binom{n}{k} = \binom{n}{n - k}$. What does this mean for the binomial distribution with $p = 0.5$?

Choosing the $k$ places for the hits also fixes the $n - k$ places for the misses. With $p = 0.5$ therefore $P(X = k) = P(X = n - k)$: the histogram is symmetric.

TEST YOURSELF!

Calculate $\binom{7}{3}$.

$\tfrac{7 \cdot 6 \cdot 5}{6} = 35$

$n = 3$, $p = 0.3$. Calculate $P(X = 1)$.

$3 \cdot 0.3 \cdot 0.7^2 = 0.441$

$n = 4$, $p = 0.2$. Calculate $P(X = 2)$.

$6 \cdot 0.04 \cdot 0.64 = 0.1536$

UNIT 28 LESSONS

2At most, at least, between

A delivery of 50 components is accepted if at most 2 are faulty. The machine produces 2% rejects. How often is a delivery accepted?

We need $P(X \le 2) = P(X = 0) + P(X = 1) + P(X = 2)$ with $n = 50$, $p = 0.02$. Such sums are called cumulative probabilities. You calculate them with the calculator (binomcdf) or read them from a table.

KEY POINT · CUMULATIVE PROBABILITIES

$P(X \le k) = \sum\limits_{i=0}^{k} \binom{n}{i} \cdot p^i \cdot (1 - p)^{n - i}$

“at least $k$”: $P(X \ge k) = 1 - P(X \le k - 1)$ · “more than $k$”: $P(X > k) = 1 - P(X \le k)$ · “fewer than $k$”: $P(X < k) = P(X \le k - 1)$

“between $a$ and $b$” (inclusive): $P(a \le X \le b) = P(X \le b) - P(X \le a - 1)$

Careful with “at least”: $P(X \ge 3) = 1 - P(X \le 2)$, not $1 - P(X \le 3)$. The 3 belongs to “at least 3”.

Check: draw the bars that are meant. The widget below colours them gold.

INTERACTIVE · THE BINOMIAL DISTRIBUTION

Set $n$ and $p$ and choose what is to be calculated. Gold are the bars that are added up. Red: the expected value, dashed: $\mu \pm \sigma$.

EXAMPLE 3 · THE DELIVERY

$n = 50$, $p = 0.02$. How likely is the delivery to be accepted? How likely is it to be completely free of faults?

$P(X \le 2) \approx 0.922$. About 92% of the deliveries are accepted.

$P(X = 0) = 0.98^{50} \approx 0.364$

EXAMPLE 4 · OVERBOOKED

103 tickets, 100 seats, every person turns up independently with 95%. How likely is it that there are not enough seats?

$X$: number of people who turn up, $n = 103$, $p = 0.95$. $P(X > 100) = 1 - P(X \le 100) \approx 0.106$. On about every tenth flight someone has to be rebooked. With 102 tickets it would only be just over 3%.

EXERCISES

$X$ is binomially distributed with $n = 20$ and $p = 0.3$. Use the widget or the calculator to find $P(X = 6)$, $P(X \le 6)$, $P(X \ge 8)$ and $P(4 \le X \le 8)$.

$0.192$; $0.608$; $0.228$; $0.780$

Translate into a probability with $X \le$: a) “at least 4”   b) “more than 4”   c) “fewer than 4”   d) “at most 4”

a) $1 - P(X \le 3)$   b) $1 - P(X \le 4)$   c) $P(X \le 3)$   d) $P(X \le 4)$

In the guessing test from example 1 you need at least 5 correct answers to pass. How likely is it to pass by guessing?

$P(X \ge 5) = 1 - P(X \le 4) \approx 0.078$. About 8% would get through.

10% of all smartphones of one model have a battery fault. In a class, 20 people have this model. How likely is it that none has the fault? At least one? At most two?

$0.9^{20} \approx 0.122$; $1 - 0.122 = 0.878$; $P(X \le 2) \approx 0.677$

How many times do you have to roll a dice at least so that at least one six comes up with a probability of at least 90%?

Solve $1 - \left(\tfrac56\right)^n \ge 0.9$, with the logarithm from Year 11 or by trial and error.

$\left(\tfrac56\right)^n \le 0.1 \Rightarrow n \ge \dfrac{\ln 0.1}{\ln \frac56} \approx 12.6$. At least 13 rolls.

$n = 10$, $p = 0.5$. Calculate $P(X \le 3)$.

$\tfrac{1 + 10 + 45 + 120}{1024} = \tfrac{176}{1024} \approx 0.1719$

UNIT 36 LESSONS

3Expected value, standard deviation and the shape of the histogram

If you roll a dice 60 times, you expect about 10 sixes. But how far may the result be from that before you become suspicious?

For the binomial distribution you do not have to calculate the expected value and the variance via the long sum: every single stage contributes $p$ to the expected value and $p(1 - p)$ to the variance. With $n$ stages this gives simple formulas.

KEY POINT · KEY FIGURES OF THE BINOMIAL DISTRIBUTION

$\mu = E(X) = n \cdot p$   ·   $V(X) = n \cdot p \cdot (1 - p)$   ·   $\sigma = \sqrt{n \cdot p \cdot (1 - p)}$

The histogram has its maximum at or next to $\mu$. The larger $n$, the wider and flatter it becomes, but in relation to $n$ ever narrower. With $p = 0.5$ it is symmetric, with small $p$ skewed to the right, with large $p$ to the left.

Rule of thumb: if $\sigma > 3$, about 68% of the values lie in the interval $[\mu - \sigma, \mu + \sigma]$.

Square root law: four times as many trials double $\sigma$. The relative spread $\tfrac{\sigma}{n}$ halves at the same time.

In the widget above the dashed lines show $\mu - \sigma$ and $\mu + \sigma$. Change $n$ and watch.

EXAMPLE 5 · ROLLING 60 TIMES

$X$: number of sixes in 60 rolls. Calculate $\mu$ and $\sigma$.

$\mu = 60 \cdot \tfrac16 = 10$, $\sigma = \sqrt{60 \cdot \tfrac16 \cdot \tfrac56} = \sqrt{8.33} \approx 2.89$. Values between about 7 and 13 are completely normal.

EXAMPLE 6 · 100 COIN TOSSES

$X$: number of heads in 100 tosses. Calculate $\mu$, $\sigma$ and $P(45 \le X \le 55)$.

$\mu = 50$, $\sigma = \sqrt{25} = 5$, $P(45 \le X \le 55) \approx 0.729$. That fits the rule of thumb well.

EXERCISES

Calculate $\mu$ and $\sigma$ for a) $n = 50$, $p = 0.1$   b) $n = 20$, $p = 0.3$   c) $n = 400$, $p = 0.5$.

a) $5$; $\sqrt{4.5} \approx 2.12$   b) $6$; $\sqrt{4.2} \approx 2.05$   c) $200$; $10$

Set $n = 20$ in the widget and compare the histograms for $p = 0.1$, $p = 0.5$ and $p = 0.9$. Describe position and shape.

$p = 0.1$: maximum at 2, skewed to the right. $p = 0.5$: symmetric about 10. $p = 0.9$: mirror image of $p = 0.1$, maximum at 18, skewed to the left.

A coin is supposed to be fair. In 100 tosses it shows heads 62 times. Is that still in the range $[\mu - 2\sigma, \mu + 2\sigma]$? What do you conclude?

$[50 - 10, 50 + 10] = [40, 60]$. 62 lies outside. That is unusual for a fair coin, it should be checked more closely. This alone does not prove anything yet.

For which $p$ is the variance $n \cdot p \cdot (1 - p)$ largest for fixed $n$? Explain without a derivative.

$p(1 - p) = p - p^2$ is a parabola opening downwards with zeros 0 and 1, its vertex is at $p = 0.5$. That is where the uncertainty is greatest.

TEST YOURSELF!

$n = 40$, $p = 0.3$. What is $\mu$?

$40 \cdot 0.3 = 12$

$n = 100$, $p = 0.1$. What is $\sigma$?

$\sqrt{100 \cdot 0.1 \cdot 0.9} = \sqrt9 = 3$

What does the histogram for $n = 30$, $p = 0.5$ look like?

With $p = 0.5$, $P(X = k) = P(X = 30 - k)$.

REVIEW · DEEPEN · CONNECT

A basketball player scores 70% of his free throws. He takes 10 shots. How many hits are to be expected? How likely is it that he scores with all of them?

$\mu = 7$; $0.7^{10} \approx 0.028$

15 people are asked, 40% of the population know a certain product. Calculate $P(X = 6)$, $P(X \le 4)$ and $P(X \ge 9)$.

$0.207$; $0.217$; $0.095$

Connecting with chapter 1.2: in the guessing test you get 1 point for every correct answer, for every wrong one $\tfrac13$ point is deducted. What score do you expect when guessing?

Per question: $1 \cdot 0.25 - \tfrac13 \cdot 0.75 = 0$. Guessing gains nothing on average, that is exactly why there is this deduction.

An airline has 100 seats and expects 95% to turn up. It wants to have too few seats on at most 5% of the flights. How many tickets may it sell? Use the widget.

With 102 tickets: $P(X > 100) \approx 0.034$, with 103 already $\approx 0.106$. At most 102 tickets.

The Galton board

The English naturalist Francis Galton built a board with many rows of pins. Balls falling from the top bounce randomly to the left or to the right at every pin. At the bottom they collect in slots, and the same bell shape appears again and again.

Explained with the binomial distribution: with $n$ rows of pins every ball is a Bernoulli chain of length $n$ with $p = 0.5$, “right” is a hit. Slot $k$ is reached via $\binom{n}{k}$ paths. With 10 rows about $\binom{10}{5} \cdot 0.5^{10} \approx 24.6\%$ of the balls land in the middle slot, in each of the two outermost ones only just under 0.1%.

Galton called his board the “quincunx” and used it to explain why many features in nature are distributed in a similar way.

Source: Francis Galton: Natural Inheritance. Macmillan, London 1889.

LOOKING BACKTHE ESSENTIALS AT A GLANCE

BERNOULLI CHAIN

$n$ independent repetitions, each a hit with probability $p$.

Roll a dice 20 times, hit: six

BINOMIAL COEFFICIENT

$\binom{n}{k} = \dfrac{n!}{k!\,(n - k)!}$ paths with exactly $k$ hits.

$\binom52 = 10$ · $\binom{49}{6} = 13{,}983{,}816$

BERNOULLI'S FORMULA

$P(X = k) = \binom{n}{k}\, p^k\, (1 - p)^{n - k}$

Guessing test: $P(X = 3) \approx 0.250$

CUMULATIVE

$P(X \ge k) = 1 - P(X \le k - 1)$ · $P(a \le X \le b) = P(X \le b) - P(X \le a - 1)$

Delivery: $P(X \le 2) \approx 0.922$

KEY FIGURES

$\mu = np$, $\sigma = \sqrt{np(1 - p)}$

Rolling 60 times: $\mu = 10$, $\sigma \approx 2.89$
